name: Unruh's Acoustic Black Hole
description: The spacetime that sound travels through in a fluid falling steadily into a point from every side. Inside $r = r_0$ the fluid falls faster than sound, so no sound gets out, and the sphere $r = r_0$ is a horizon that should glow with thermal sound. It solves no field equation of gravity, and its horizon has been made in a Bose-Einstein condensate.
convention: Here $c$ is the speed of sound in the fluid, constant throughout it, and it stands wherever the speed of light does in a spacetime of gravity; we keep it explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Water forced through a narrow nozzle can be made to run faster than sound, and in the fast stretch a sound wave is dragged downstream whichever way it points [barcelo2011]. William Unruh, a physicist at the University of British Columbia, saw a black hole in that stretch, with a horizon for sound where the flow passes the speed of sound [unruh1981]. Black hole evaporation was, in his words, "one of the most surprising discoveries of the past ten years", and its derivation assumed, among other things, that the wave equation of the radiated field holds on every scale [unruh1981]. Testing any of it seemed to need a small black hole, "a relic of the initial stages in the life of the universe perhaps", found near the Earth [unruh1981]. So he put a question mark in his title, "Experimental Black-Hole Evaporation?" [unruh1981].¶Unruh's fluid flows without vorticity, and its pressure depends on its density alone [unruh1981]. A small ripple on a steady flow of it, followed through its velocity potential, obeys the equation of a massless scalar field in a curved spacetime, whose metric is built from the density $\rho$, the velocity $\mathbf{v}$ of the flow, and the speed of sound $c$ [unruh1981]. Vincent Moncrief had met a metric of the same kind a year earlier, for sound in gas falling onto a Schwarzschild black hole, and found a "sound horizon" outside the black hole's own, "across which the flow becomes supersonic" [moncrief1980]. He used it to show that such accretion is stable, with "no unstable normal modes" reaching outside the sound horizon [moncrief1980]. Carlos Barceló, Stefano Liberati, and Matt Visser count Moncrief's work a precursor of acoustic horizons, written for the stability of accretion, and find that "there seems to have not been any cross-connection" between it and Unruh's [barcelo2011].¶For his black hole Unruh took a flow that is spherically symmetric, steady, and converging on a point, with the speed of sound held constant "for simplicity" [unruh1981]. The flow carries every wave inward with it, which in the laboratory's time $t$ shows as a cross term in $dt\,dr$, and Unruh took it out with a time of his own, $\tau = t + \int v\,dr/(c^2 - v^2)$, $v$ being the radial velocity of the flow [unruh1981]. In $\tau$ the metric is $(\rho/c)\left[-(c^2 - v^2)\,d\tau^2 + c^2dr^2/(c^2 - v^2) + r^2d\Omega^2\right]$, and near the radius $R$ where the inflow passes $c$, with $v = -c + \alpha(r - R)$, it takes the form of Schwarzschild's metric near its horizon [unruh1981, visser1998]. The time $\tau$, he added, "has no physical significance except for the small-amplitude sonic motions of the medium" [unruh1981]. A real transsonic flow generally develops a shock, which Unruh proposed to smooth away with external forces or "a suitably shaped nozzle" [unruh1981]. Spherical symmetry is not essential either: in his words, a nozzle "gives exactly the same results" [unruh1981].¶Unruh then quantized the sound outside the horizon, taking its state to be the vacuum for an observer carried through the horizon by the fluid [unruh1981]. Near the horizon the outgoing modes behave as a scalar field's do near Schwarzschild's, so the hole glows: it gives out sound with a thermal spectrum at $T = (\hbar/2\pi k_B)\,\partial v/\partial r$, taken at the horizon, the counterpart of $\hbar c^3/(8\pi k_BGM)$ for a black hole of mass $M$ [unruh1981]. With a speed of sound of $300$ m/s and a horizon $1$ mm in radius, his estimate came to $3\times10^{-7}$ K, "probably undetectable in the presence of turbulent instabilities", though still "a much simpler experimental task than creating a $10^{-8}$-cm black hole" [unruh1981]. The fluid's equations fail at atomic distances, about $10^{-8}$ cm, much as a smooth spacetime is expected to fail near $10^{-33}$ cm, which makes the sonic hole, in Unruh's words, "an excellent theoretical laboratory" for what quantum gravity might do to evaporation [unruh1981]. Theodore Jacobson took up that question a decade later, discussing "the role played by ultrahigh frequencies or ultrashort distances in the usual derivations of the Hawking effect", and built Unruh's fluid into a model of it [jacobson1991, barcelo2011].¶How fast should the fluid fall? Unruh left that open, with $v$ any function that passes $-c$ smoothly at the horizon [unruh1981]. A fluid of constant density gives the simplest answer, since continuity alone then makes the inward speed fall as $1/r^2$, $v = -c\,r_0^2/r^2$, with the horizon at $r = r_0$ [visser1998]. Matt Visser called the result "the canonical acoustic black hole", with the metric $-(1 - r_0^4/r^4)\,c^2d\tau^2 + dr^2/(1 - r_0^4/r^4) + r^2d\Omega^2$ in Unruh's time, which "is not any of the standard geometries typically considered in general relativity" [visser1998]. At the horizon the speed of the inflow changes by $2c/r_0$ per unit of radius, so Unruh's formula puts its temperature at $\hbar c/(\pi k_Br_0)$ [unruh1981, visser1998]. A horizon that lasts would take a big tank of fluid drained supersonically through a long thin pipe to its centre, which Visser judged "a technologically challenging project" [visser1998].¶At the Technion in Haifa, Jeff Steinhauer made the horizon a sharp step in the potential of a laser, swept along a Bose-Einstein condensate of rubidium atoms [steinhauer2016]. Upstream of the step the condensate flowed at $0.24$ mm/s, slower than its sound at $0.57$ mm/s, and beyond it at $1.02$ mm/s, faster than its sound at $0.25$ mm/s, so phonons there could not reach the horizon [steinhauer2016]. He saw correlations between Hawking particles outside and their partners inside, and found that "the high-energy pairs are entangled, while the low-energy pairs are not" [steinhauer2016]. Three years later Juan Ramón Muñoz de Nova, Katrine Golubkov, Victor Kolobov, and Steinhauer found the spectrum of those correlations thermal, with a temperature "given by the surface gravity", which for a constant speed of sound is $c$ times the slope $\partial v/\partial r$ in Unruh's formula [munozdenova2019, visser1998].

related.text: The same idea in two dimensions, water swirling down a drain, which gives sound an ergoregion outside its horizon. Unruh's fluid falls straight in, so its ergosurface lies on its horizon [visser1998].

Near its horizon Unruh's metric takes the form of Schwarzschild's near his, and its temperature follows the same law. Away from the horizon they part: the canonical fluid falls as $1/r^2$, where Painlevé and Gullstrand's space falls as $1/\sqrt{r}$ [unruh1981, visser1998].
The same form, flat space with a flow through it. Natário's shift vector is the fluid's velocity here, and his $c$ is the speed of sound [natario2002, visser1998].
Another flat space with a flow through it, a bubble carried along by its shift vector. Here the flow is a fluid falling into a point, and $c$ is the speed of sound [alcubierre1994, visser1998].
The fluid with no flow, $r_0 = 0$: flat spacetime with the speed of sound for its $c$ [visser1998].

coordinates.name: Laboratory

parameters.description: Radius of the sonic horizon, where the fluid falls inward at the speed of sound: the fluid's radial velocity is $-c\,r_0^2/r^2$

coordinates.convention: We use the laboratory's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$: its time $t$, carrying dimensions of time, and spherical coordinates centred on the sink. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{2r_0^4\left(r + r_0\right)\left(r - r_0\right)\left(r^2 + r_0^2\right)}{r^9}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{4r_0^6}{r^7}\dot{t}\dot{r} - \dfrac{2r_0^4}{r^5}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r + r_0\right)\left(r - r_0\right)\left(r^2 + r_0^2\right)}{r^3}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r + r_0\right)\left(r - r_0\right)\left(r^2 + r_0^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{r^3}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Unruh's Time

parameters.description: Radius of the sonic horizon, where the fluid falls inward at the speed of sound: the fluid's radial velocity is $-c\,r_0^2/r^2$

coordinates.convention: We use Unruh's time $\tau$ outside the horizon, with $c\,d\tau = c\,dt - r_0^2r^2\,dr/(r^4 - r_0^4)$ for the laboratory's $t$, so that the metric has no cross term. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{2r_0^4\left(r + r_0\right)\left(r - r_0\right)\left(r^2 + r_0^2\right)}{r^9}\dot{\tau}^2 - \dfrac{2r_0^4}{r\left(r + r_0\right)\left(r - r_0\right)\left(r^2 + r_0^2\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r + r_0\right)\left(r - r_0\right)\left(r^2 + r_0^2\right)}{r^3}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r + r_0\right)\left(r - r_0\right)\left(r^2 + r_0^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{r^3}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
